ambient_occlusion — 3D render op

• Data kinds: mesh → image2d

• Call: import fullseye as fs; fs.ledger.ambient_occlusion(V, F, pose=None, intrinsics=None, width: 'int' = 256, height: 'int' = 256, n_dirs: 'int' = 64, max_dist: 'float | None' = None, k: 'int' = 3, background: 'float' = 1.0, method: 'str' = 'auto') -> 'np.ndarray' (to call the implementation directly, import render_ao; render_ao.ambient_occlusion(V, F, pose=None, intrinsics=None, width: 'int' = 256, height: 'int' = 256, n_dirs: 'int' = 64, max_dist: 'float | None' = None, k: 'int' = 3, background: 'float' = 1.0, method: 'str' = 'auto') -> 'np.ndarray'; from the registry, ops3d.get("ambient_occlusion"))

Usage

Render the mesh into an AO map image (H, W) in [0,1].

Obtains depth / silhouette / triangle id and perspective-corrected barycentric coordinates with render3d.render_mesh (rasterisation and hidden-surface removal are left to it, not reinvented), and bakes in the per-vertex AO of the object-space vertex_occlusion by barycentric interpolation from the 3 vertices of the triangle covering that pixel. Outside the object (silhouette=0) is background (default 1.0 = fully exposed). When *pose* / *intrinsics* are omitted, render3d.auto_view frames the view. fail-closed validation follows the lower-level functions.

k is unused since 2026-09-02 (kept for backward compatibility). Until then it looked up the nearest k vertices in camera space and mixed them with inverse-distance weights, but on surfaces with coarse vertices this gave polygonal cells, which showed up as a mottled pattern on the ground of the article's hero image. Barycentric interpolation is an exact linear interpolation inside the triangle, so it is continuous regardless of vertex density, and it never picks up vertices of a different, adjacent object.
